extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated coal-fired EGU owners/operators, industry stakeholders, and EPA rulewriters/analysts
extracted.subtask_short: EPA BSER determination for coal EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and justificatory criteria used by EPA to determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and subcategorize existing coal-fired steam generating units (e.g., long-term vs. medium-term), including technical demonstration, cost reasonableness, non-air quality impacts, and reporting requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement That Source Must Transfer CO2 to an Entity That Reports Under the GHGRP
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires that EGUs that capture CO2 in order to meet the applicable emission standard report in accordance with the GHGRP requirements of 40 CFR part 98, including subpart PP. If injection occurs on site, the EGU must report data accordingly under 40 CFR part 98 subpart RR or subpart VV. If the CO2 is injected off site, the EGU must transfer the captured CO2 to a facility that reports in accordance with the requirements of 40 CFR part 98, subpart RR or subpart VV. They may also transfer the captured CO2 to a facility that has received an innovative technology waiver from the EPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GHGRP subpart RR and subpart VV provide monitoring and reporting mechanisms to quantify CO2 storage and to identify, quantify, and address potential leakage. Under existing GHGRP regulations, sequestration wells permitted as Class VI under the UIC program are required to report under subpart RR. Facilities with UIC Class II wells that inject CO2 to enhance recovery can opt-in to reporting under subpart RR by submitting and receiving approval for an MRV plan. Subpart VV applies to facilities that conduct enhanced recovery using ISO 27916 unless they opted into subpart RR.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER Evaluation Factors (How EPA Chooses 'Best')
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining BSER, EPA weighs multiple factors to select the 'best' system of emission reduction from among adequately demonstrated options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factors include whether the system is adequately demonstrated, cost reasonableness (including amortization period), unit-level emission reductions (degree of emission limitation), applicability/widespread use, energy requirements, and non-air quality health and environmental impacts. EPA selects the system that best balances these criteria for the source category or subcategory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately Demonstrated (CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS with 90 percent capture is 'adequately demonstrated' for long-term coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes historical use of solvent-based CO2 capture, thousands of miles of CO2 pipelines, tens of millions of tons of CO2 permanently stored, at least 15 operating U.S. CCS projects and many more under development, and commercial-scale examples (Boundary Dam Unit 3, Petra Nova) that have achieved ~90% capture. Legal precedent allows EPA to rely on commercial-scale data and extrapolate to similar sources; specific technological improvements support expectation of 90% capture broadly. Transport and geologic storage have likewise been demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Reasonableness (CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates whether the costs of CCS are 'reasonable' to determine if CCS may be BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations include recent process improvements reducing projected costs, accounting for relevant incentives such as the IRC section 45Q tax credit ($85/metric ton), amortization period assumptions (e.g., 12-year amortization, 80% capacity factor), source-specific transport and storage costs, and model projections (IPM) showing some deployment even absent the rule. EPA compares $/ton CO2 reduced and $/MWh to costs for other controls to assess reasonableness (example: average total costs of CCS could be −$5/ton and −$4/MWh for certain fleets when accounting for 45Q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-Air Quality Health and Environmental Impacts and Energy Requirements (CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses potential non-air quality impacts and energy demands of CCS and whether they militates against designating CCS as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture plants require pretreatment to remove SO2 and PM and controls to limit solvent degradation/loss. Regulatory frameworks (state-level controls, PHMSA pipeline safety, UIC Class VI under SDWA, GHGRP subpart RR) mitigate non-GHG risks. Capture plants require steam and electricity, impacting energy use, but 45Q incentives may increase total generation; EPA concluded energy requirements are not unreasonable and adverse impacts are limited and mitigable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial Capture CCS Not BSER (Why Rejected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial capture CCS was not determined to be BSER because emission reductions are lower and costs would generally be higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 90% capture captures very high absolute emissions and benefits from economies of scale; partial capture would miss large emissions volumes and receive fewer benefits from IRC section 45Q (credits tied to amount sequestered), making $/ton costs higher. Therefore partial capture fails to balance BSER criteria as well as 90% CCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Gas Co-Firing Considerations (BSER vs Not BSER)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluated 40% natural gas co-firing as an emissions reduction option and determined it is BSER for medium-term units but not for long-term units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For medium-term units (those ceasing operation by Jan 1, 2039), 40% co-firing is adequately demonstrated, has reasonable energy/non-air impacts, achievable infrastructure by Jan 1, 2030, and is cost-reasonable; it yields ~16% stack emission rate reductions. For long-term units, 40% co-firing was not selected because CCS achieves substantially greater unit-level emission reductions (88.4% vs 16%) and CCS otherwise matches up well against BSER criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Rate Improvements (HRI) Not BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat rate improvements were not considered BSER for long-term steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found achievable reductions from HRI are very low, many sources have already implemented HRI (leaving limited additional reductions), and there is potential for a rebound effect increasing total emissions. Additionally, reductions from efficiency improvements would not be additive to CCS due to capture plant impacts on net efficiency (steam and electricity load).

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER Must Achieve Significant Unit-Level Emission Reductions Where Relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA takes into account the magnitude of emission reductions achievable at the unit level when weighing BSER options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individual coal-fired power plants are among the highest-emitting sources, EPA gives weight to technologies (e.g., 90% CCS) that remove very large absolute quantities of CO2 at the unit level compared to options (e.g., 40% co-firing) that yield much smaller unit-level reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorization by Operating Horizon (Legal Basis and Rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may identify subcategories of sources based on relevant characteristics (including operating horizon) that affect what controls are 'best' for those subcategories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operating horizon affects amortization period and thus the annualized cost of controls; EPA's authority under CAA section 111(d) and precedent allows subcategorization by cost-of-control-relevant factors (analogous to prior subcategories by load level or fuel type). The EPA used operating-horizon subcategories (imminent/near/medium/long-term concepts) to set BSER appropriate for sources that plan to cease operation earlier. States retain authority to consider remaining useful life (RULOF) for individual sources in state plan application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Rationale for Medium-Term Coal-Fired Subcategory
rubrics_metrics.description: Medium-term coal-fired steam generating units are those demonstrating they plan to permanently cease operation after December 31, 2031 and before January 1, 2039; EPA finalized 40% natural gas co-firing as BSER for this subcategory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a large share of units have announced retirements by 2039; CCS is capital-intensive and requires longer amortization to be cost-reasonable, whereas 40% co-firing has lower capital costs, can be implemented by Jan 1, 2030, and yields costs (example: $73/ton CO2 reduced or $13/MWh for a 9-year amortization) that are comparable to other control cost metrics ($10.60-$18.50/MWh) and prior GHG metrics (e.g., 2016 NSPS $98/ton CO2e). The medium-term subcategory is elective and states may use RULOF to set less stringent standards for individual units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately Demonstrated (Natural Gas Co-Firing at 40%)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined that natural gas co-firing at 40% of annual heat input is adequately demonstrated for coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes widespread existing use of natural gas at coal units (249 of 565 units reported consuming natural gas in 2021), observed hourly and annual co-firing rates (29 units co-fired >=60% hourly; 29 units co-fired >40% annual), and technical feasibility via boiler modifications. EPA also assessed natural gas pipeline availability and potential lateral pipeline construction to support increased co-firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler Modifications and Efficiency Impacts for Co-Firing
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing boilers can be modified to co-fire natural gas (up to 100%) by installing new gas burners and related equipment, but introduction of natural gas can slightly affect boiler efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical modifications: new burners, new fuel supply lines, modifications to air ducts. Net heat rate impact can range from a 2% increase to a 2% decrease; reductions in coal use can reduce auxiliary power demand which offsets some impacts. The existing practice of multi-fuel capability and historical examples of high-hourly co-firing support feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Gas Pipeline Development Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: To enable higher levels of natural gas co-firing, plants may need to connect to the natural gas transmission network via lateral pipelines; cost depends on length, size, number of laterals and plant proximity to existing pipelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. network has ~3 million miles of pipelines; EPA estimated costs of developing lateral capacity sufficient to meet 60% of net summer capacity for candidate units. Pipeline capacity, siting, and distance to transmission lines are key factors in feasibility and cost assessments for co-firing infrastructure.
